newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FOCUS-Petron says forex exposure not a concern.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Petron says forex exposure not a concern.

text.p: The Philippines' biggest oil firm, Petron Corp, is unlikely to be hit by the removal of government-provided foreign exchange cover as the peso/dollar rate is stable, chairman Monico Jacob said on Wednesday.

"Right now the peso-dollar is very stable, so it is possible for us to continue with our 120 (day), 180-day (dollar) borrowing," Jacob told reporters after addressing local businessmen on the effects of deregulation on the oil industry.

One of the effects of the deregulation, which came into effect on February 8, is that the government has withdrawn the risk cover it used to give the industry for its foreign exchange costs in oil imports.
Asked if Petron saw a need for hedging its foreign exchange exposure, Jacob said the company could currently do without forward cover.
"With the peso stable, we can chance it that there will be no substantial fluctuation and borrow right away for 120 days. It is not a problem," Jacob said.
At present, Petron's monthly foreign exchange requirement was around $80 million, Jacob said.
Petron, which used to be state owned, is 40 percent held by Saudi Arabia's Aramco.
For the Philippines' three oil firms, deregulation has thrown up the prospects of fierce competition from existing as well as new players and in the short-term pricing will be the main weapon.
With crude oil imports comprising almost 60 percent of the oil firms' costs, volatility in the foreign exchange markets could affect their ability to offer competitive prices.

The pricing strategies of each company would be led by the production costs, the exchange rate and the efficiency of each firm's distribution network, but the determining factor would be what the competition was doing, Jacob said.

Reinier Williams, president of Petron's rival Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp, said the oil firms' margins were very narrow which meant there could not be much of difference between the prices offered by the competing firms.
Pilipinas Shell is a unit of the Royal Dutch/Shell group of companies.
The third oil refiner in the Philippines is Caltex Philippines, a unit of Chevron Corp and Texaco Inc.

Since the government pushed ahead with the oil industry's deregulation in the face of opposition from some left-wing groups which said fuel prices would surge, the three oil companies have been subject to acute scrutiny.
Some newspapers have said the companies could form a cartel to raise prices.
"This (a cartel) is not possible because with deregulation new entrants will come in," Jacob said.
